name: Karl Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the acute medical admissions unit at Saltmere Hospital, on the coast. It's where people come up from the emergency department before they get a proper ward bed: chest pains, falls, infections, people who are just very unwell and nobody's sure why yet. Twelve-hour shifts, four or five patients each, constant turnover. I'm also on the hospital's digital working group, so one afternoon a fortnight I'm trialling the AI note-taker that listens to handover and writes it up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace and I like the puzzle, working out who's actually sick. I use AI every day: on the trial, but also on my own phone to check drug interactions against the formulary and to summarise guidelines. What wears me out is money. I share a house with two others near the harbour, I've got a student loan and a motorbike on finance, and I'm on the bottom of the pay band for my grade. There aren't many hospitals round here, so if Saltmere doesn't work out, I'd have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype, a few routine tasks. Honestly, that would be a bit of a let-down for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was surprised, because the tools I use are genuinely good at small things. I'd post something on the digital group's chat about not throwing away the bits that work. I'd be the annoying one saying "it saved us ten minutes a shift, that's not nothing".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd actually be a bit disappointed. I've spent a year learning these tools and the payoff would be a slightly faster handover. I'd hoped digital nursing could be my way up to a better-paid job, and in this picture that path gets a lot narrower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts on admissions and stay on the working group, because the small wins still count. I'd look at applying for the band above mine on the unit within a year, the old-fashioned way, through experience. I'd keep riding the motorbike to save on fuel and stop the gym membership I barely use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, a bit. Not scared at all about the job, just stuck about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the small win you'd be sad to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The note-taker writing up handover. Last week it caught that Mr Okafor (a patient on the unit) had an allergy we'd all missed on the paper sheet. That's worth something, even if it's not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the path to better pay narrows. What's plan B?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plan B is boring: get the experience, go for the next grade, maybe an intensive care course. It's slower and it pays less than I'd hoped. I'd probably have to stay in the shared house till I'm 30.

say: I'd say the tools are genuinely good at **small things** and worth keeping.
I'd remind the digital group that **ten minutes** saved a shift still counts.
think: I'd be **disappointed** after a year spent learning tools with a small payoff.
My hoped-for route into **better-paid digital nursing** gets much narrower.
do: Stay on the **digital working group** and keep the small wins going.
Apply for the **next pay band** on the unit within a year through experience.
Drop the **gym membership** and keep using the motorbike to save fuel.
feel: **Flat**, with no fear about the job itself.
**Stuck** about money, likely sharing a house until he's 30.
S0.quote: I'd actually be a bit disappointed. I've spent a year learning these tools and the payoff would be a slightly faster handover.
fieldNote: He's one of the few who'd be **let down** by AI failing, because it was his career route.
His job feels safe; the unease is about **pay** and a shared house he wants to leave.

steps.text: Keep working admissions shifts and stay on the digital working group
Apply for the next pay band on the unit within a year
Cancel the gym membership and keep riding the motorbike

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I've been expecting. That's basically what the working group thinks will happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get nurses away from the computer and back to patients, if we do it right. I'd also say loudly that the union has to negotiate how the time saved gets used. Otherwise it just becomes an excuse to run the unit with fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI note-taker gives me back forty minutes a shift, and I want the union to make sure those forty minutes go to patients, not to cuts. For me personally it's a good picture. Somebody has to set these systems up and check them, and I'd like that somebody to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the clinical digital nurse post the hospital's been talking about, the moment it's advertised. I'd do the free online course in health data that the university runs, evenings, three months. And I'd ask the union rep to put AI on the agenda at the next branch meeting, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous that I'd be seen as management's tech guy by the other nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerks and the discharge coordinators. A lot of what they do is booking, phoning and chasing forms, which is exactly what the card says goes first. I'd hate to be the guy who set up the system that did them out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited but money's tight. Does a new post actually change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A digital nurse post would be a grade up, maybe 300 more a month after tax. That's the difference between the shared house and my own little flat. So yes, but only if the post really happens and doesn't go to someone already senior.

say: I'd say AI can get nurses **back to patients** if it's done right.
I'd insist the **union negotiates** how saved time gets used, so it isn't used for cuts.
think: For me this is a **good picture**, because someone has to set up and check these systems.
I want the **forty minutes** saved per shift to go to patients, not staff cuts.
do: Apply for the **clinical digital nurse** post the moment it's advertised.
Take the university's free **health data course** over three months of evenings.
Ask the union rep to put **AI on the agenda** at the next branch meeting.
feel: **Excited** about a role he's been building towards.
**Nervous** about being seen as management's tech guy by colleagues.
S1.quote: The AI note-taker gives me back forty minutes a shift, and I want the union to make sure those forty minutes go to patients, not to cuts.
fieldNote: He sees this picture as **his opportunity**, but worries about clerks and discharge coordinators.
His progressive streak shows: he wants **union control** over time saved by AI.
Money keeps him uneasy rather than calm; the new post is **not guaranteed**.

steps.text: Apply for the clinical digital nurse post when it's advertised
Take the university's free health data course over three months
Ask the union rep to put AI on the branch meeting agenda

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's two years. And robots in 2031. Okay, that flips it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public control of these systems and a guaranteed income, fast, because two years is nothing for a hospital. I'd be pushing the union and writing to anyone who'd listen. Online I'd say it's not the technology, it's who owns it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the job I'm training for, checking the AI, gets done by a better AI. I'd be retraining for something that expires. The hands-on part of admissions, cannulas, catheters, calming people down, gives me until 2031, and that's the bit I'd have to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop chasing the digital post and get every hands-on skill I can: cannulation sign-off, the advanced life support course, maybe the intensive care course next spring. I'd sign up for paid work testing clinical AI for one of the companies, a few hours a week from home, to build some savings. I'd also start looking at hospitals in the city, because Saltmere might shrink first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I'm normally the calm one about this stuff, so it's strange to feel the ground move under me too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for someone with your mix of screen and hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My day's maybe a third screens and two thirds hands. The screen third goes in 2028, which honestly I'd hand over gladly. The hands two-thirds gives me three years, which is enough to save something but not enough to retrain into a whole new field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do paid work testing the very systems you're worried about. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, completely. But I'd rather the person testing them is a nurse who's seen a real deteriorating patient. And I need the money, so I'm not going to pretend I'm above it.

say: I'd call for **public control** of these systems and a guaranteed income, fast.
I'd say the problem is **who owns** the technology, not the technology itself.
think: By 2028 a better AI does the **checking job** I'm training for.
My **hands-on skills** give me until 2031, and I'd have to lean on them.
do: Get **hands-on sign-offs**: cannulation, advanced life support, then the intensive care course.
Take a few hours a week of paid **AI testing work** from home.
Start looking at **city hospitals** in case Saltmere shrinks first.
feel: **Unsettled**, which is unusual for someone normally calm about technology.
A strange feeling of the **ground moving** under him too.
S2.quote: By 2028 the job I'm training for, checking the AI, gets done by a better AI. I'd be retraining for something that expires.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **reverses his strategy**, from digital roles back to hands-on skills.
He names the **contradiction** of testing AI for money and owns it honestly.
He splits his day as **a third screens**, two thirds hands, and plans around it.

steps.text: Get cannulation sign-off and the advanced life support course
Take paid clinical AI testing work a few hours a week
Apply to city hospitals in case Saltmere shrinks
Lobby the union for public control of hospital AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for AGI, robots around 2034. Five years is a different game from two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hospital needs a five-year plan for staff, with nurses writing it. I'd be the one volunteering to help write it. I'd keep the public-ownership line, but I'd focus on practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the digital post isn't a dead end, it's a stepping stone. With five years, I'd aim to be the nurse who tells the robot company what a real night shift looks like. I'd be about 35 when robots arrive, which is young enough to pivot again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the digital post if it came up, and do a part-time postgraduate certificate in health informatics, paid for by the hospital if I can argue for it. I'd keep a small side income testing AI tools. And I'd get the union and the working group in the same room, which has never happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but busy. Like the start of a long shift when you can already see it'll be heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your housemates about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One's a delivery driver and one works in a call centre, so honestly they'd be in worse shape than me. I'd probably end up helping the call centre one find a course. That's kind of my thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the digital post went to someone else, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd apply in the city and move. I'm not tied down here, no kids, no mortgage. That's the one advantage of having nothing.

I'd volunteer to help write it and keep a **practical** focus.

S3.quote: With five years, I'd aim to be the nurse who tells the robot company what a real night shift looks like.
fieldNote: With five years he sees a **path forward**, so his mood steadies to uneasy.
He frames having **no ties** as a strength, a rare upside to a thin cushion.
He'd help his **housemates** too, especially the call centre worker.

steps.text: Start a part-time health informatics certificate
Keep testing clinical AI tools for extra income
Bring the union and digital working group together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036 and robots around 2039. Ten years. I'd be 37 when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually do it well: proper rules, nurses trained, a public say over the systems. I'd be campaigning for that, but with a smile, not a placard. People listen more when you're not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to go from a shared house to running the digital side of a hospital, if I don't waste it. That's genuinely exciting. The money's still tight now, but a decade is time to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the informatics master's part-time within two years, once I've cleared the motorbike finance. I'd volunteer to lead the rollout of the next AI tools on admissions. And I'd stand for a seat on the hospital's staff council, so nurses have a voice on how it's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Hopeful. The first one of these where I feel like I'm in front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older nurses on nights who don't like screens. Ten years is plenty for me but some of them are tired. I'd want the hospital to give them real training time, not a video at 3am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "if I don't waste it". What would wasting it look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Letting the digital group fizzle, not doing the master's, telling myself I've got time. I've seen it happen to people who were keen at 25.

say: I'd say this version lets us do it well, with **rules and training** for nurses.
I'd campaign for a **public say** over the systems, calmly rather than angrily.
think: Ten years could take me from a **shared house** to running a hospital's digital side.
Money is **still tight** now, but a decade gives me time to climb.
do: Start a part-time **informatics master's** within two years, after clearing the bike finance.
Volunteer to **lead the rollout** of new AI tools on admissions.
Stand for a seat on the hospital's **staff council**.
feel: **Hopeful**, the first picture where he feels ahead of the change.
A touch of **caution** that comfort could waste the decade.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to go from a shared house to running the digital side of a hospital, if I don't waste it.
fieldNote: The change **looks good for him** here; his mood is calm despite a thin cushion.
He wants **real training time** for older night nurses, not videos at 3am.
His main fear is **complacency**, not the technology.

steps.text: Start an informatics master's after clearing the motorbike finance
Volunteer to lead the AI tool rollout on admissions
Stand for a seat on the hospital's staff council

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, which surprises people, because they think I'm the tech fan. Two years is too short for me to get anywhere useful, and the digital route I've built closes fast. Everyone assumes the nerdy nurse is happy about AI. I'm happy about the tools. I'm worried about who owns them. What would help is the hospital paying for proper training and a guarantee that time saved by AI stays with patients.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about housing. Half the young nurses I know can't afford to live near the hospital. If jobs move, we can't follow them, and if they stay, we can't afford to stay with them.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes the nerdy nurse is happy about AI. I'm happy about the tools. I'm worried about who owns them.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old admissions nurse** at a coastal hospital who uses AI every day.
He sits on the hospital's **digital working group** and hoped it would be his route to better pay.
He shares a house, rides a motorbike on finance and has **almost no savings**.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** and pushes him back to hands-on skills; slower pictures make him hopeful.
He wants **public control** of AI and union say over the time it saves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his digital career route would close before he reached it.
whatWouldHelp: The hospital **paying for training** and a guarantee that time saved by AI goes to patients.
